title: Day-hike essentials checklist
context: The day-hike essentials are the few items that let you get through an unplanned night: navigation, light, sun protection, first aid, a knife, fire, shelter, extra food, extra water, and extra clothes. Also called ten essentials, what to bring hiking, hiking checklist, day pack list. Look for map and compass as well as a phone; headlamp with spare batteries. Pack the same essentials for every hike, even a short one, and leave a trip plan with someone at home.

title: Deer-hunt day kit
context: A deer-hunt day kit covers the hunt itself, getting an animal out, and getting yourself home: license and tags, orange, a sharp knife, gloves, a drag rope, light, water, and first aid. Also called what to bring deer hunting, hunting pack list, deer hunting gear checklist. Look for license, tags, and a pen or zip ties for tagging; hunter orange hat and vest.

title: 72-hour bag, car kit, and home outage kit
context: A 72-hour kit holds what each person needs for three days without help: water, food, light, radio, first aid, medicines, warmth, copies of documents, and cash. Also called go bag, bug out bag, 72 hour kit, emergency kit, car emergency kit. Look for a gallon of water per person per day; a week of prescription medicines where possible.

title: Forgot your knife, light, or fire starter
context: When a key item is left behind, safer substitutes and a changed plan beat improvising something risky: a phone light in short bursts, a multi-tool or sharp-edged stone, and turning back before dark. Also called forgot my knife, no flashlight, forgot lighter, no fire starter, improvise gear. Look for phone battery level; how much daylight is left. Shorten the trip, start back early, save phone battery for calls and short light, and borrow from a partner.

title: Clothing layers: wool and synthetics versus cotton
context: Layers let you adjust warmth: a base layer that moves sweat, an insulating layer, and a wind and rain shell; wool and synthetics stay warm when damp, while wet cotton pulls heat away fast. Also called layering, cotton kills, what to wear hiking, wool vs cotton, base layer. Look for cotton jeans or a cotton hoodie on a cold, wet day; shivering when you stop.

title: Headlamp, spare batteries, and red mode
context: A headlamp keeps your hands free; spare batteries or a charged backup, and a dim red mode that protects night vision, make it last the night. Also called headlamp, red light mode, spare batteries, flashlight for camping. Look for batteries tested before the trip; a red or dim setting. Carry a headlamp and spares on every outing, keep batteries warm in cold weather, and use red mode around camp and when reading a map.

title: Knife safety and a basic edge
context: Safe knife use means cutting away from your body and others, keeping a blood circle clear around you, and keeping the blade sharp so it does not slip. Also called knife safety, sharpen a knife, cut away from yourself, dull knife. Look for a clear arm's length around you; a firm grip and a stable work surface. Cut away from your body, close or sheath the knife when not using it, and sharpen at a steady, shallow angle on a stone or rod.

title: Water filter care
context: Hollow-fiber water filters must be kept from freezing once wet, because ice can crack the fibers without any visible sign and let germs through. Also called hollow fiber filter frozen, sawyer filter care, backflush filter, water filter cold. Look for a filter used on a cold trip; slower flow over time. In freezing weather keep a used filter in an inside pocket and in your sleeping bag at night, and backflush it as the maker directs.

title: First-aid kit contents
context: A useful first-aid kit matches your trip and training: bandages and gauze, tape, gloves, blister care, pain relievers, personal medicines, and for bleeding, pressure dressings and a commercial tourniquet if you have trained with it. Also called first aid kit list, what to put in a first aid kit, trauma kit, IFAK. Look for personal medicines and an epinephrine auto-injector if prescribed; gloves and a pressure dressing.

title: Stove and fuel safety
context: Camp stoves and fuel are safe used outdoors in open air, set on a stable surface away from tents and brush, with fuel stored cool and closed. Also called camp stove safety, propane safety, white gas stove, cooking in a tent. Look for a stable, flat base; no tent fabric, overhanging branches, or dry grass nearby. Cook outside, light the stove before leaning over it, let it cool before refueling, and pack fuel apart from food.

title: Boot fit and blister prevention
context: Blisters come from friction, heat, and moisture; boots that fit, dry socks, and treating hot spots early prevent most of them. Also called blisters hiking, hiking boot fit, hot spot on foot, prevent blisters. Look for a warm, rubbing hot spot; heel lifting in the boot. Break boots in before a trip, wear wool or synthetic socks, stop at the first hot spot, and cover it with tape or moleskin.

title: Sleeping bag temperature ratings
context: A sleeping bag's temperature rating is a lab estimate; most people need a bag rated colder than the night, plus an insulated pad under them. Also called sleeping bag rating, how warm a sleeping bag, sleeping pad R value, cold at night camping. Look for the comfort versus limit rating; a pad's insulation (R-value) for cold ground. Choose a bag rated below the expected low, add a warm pad, wear a dry hat and base layer, and eat before bed.

title: Fitting a backpack
context: A pack fits when the hip belt carries most of the weight on the hip bones and the shoulder straps hug without carrying the load. Also called backpack fit, hip belt, pack hurts shoulders, adjust a pack. Look for hip belt centered on the hip bones; load lifters snug at an angle. Loosen everything, buckle the hip belt first, then snug the shoulder straps, load lifters, and sternum strap. Pack heavy items close to your spine.

title: Field repair: tape, cord, and needle
context: A small repair kit of tape, cord, a needle and strong thread, safety pins, and a few zip ties fixes most broken straps, torn shells, and gear failures. Also called repair kit, fix a torn jacket, broken strap, duct tape repair. Look for duct or repair tape wrapped on a bottle or pole; spare cord and a buckle. Patch holes with tape on both sides, sew or pin torn straps, lash broken parts with cord, and keep a wet sleeping bag in a dry bag.

title: Rope and cordage basics
context: A length of strong cord lets you hang a tarp, rig a clothesline, lash a splint, or hang food; knowing a few knots makes it useful. Also called paracord, what rope to carry, cordage, rope for camping. Look for about 50 feet of thin, strong cord; rope rated for the job if it holds people. Carry cord for camp jobs and learn a bowline, a taut-line hitch, and two half hitches.

title: Binoculars and rangefinders in practice
context: Binoculars help you identify animals and people before acting; a rangefinder measures distance to keep shots within your practiced range. Also called binoculars, rangefinder, glassing, how far is that deer. Look for a steady rest when glassing; identifying the whole animal. Glass from a rest, range a few landmarks around your stand, and use binoculars, not a rifle scope, to look at things you are not sure of.

title: Trekking poles
context: Trekking poles take strain off knees on descents, add balance on stream crossings and ice, and can hold up a tarp. Also called hiking poles, walking sticks, trekking pole height. Look for elbow at about a right angle on flat ground; longer for downhill, shorter for uphill. Adjust the length to the slope, use the straps correctly, and plant poles ahead on crossings.

title: Saw and hatchet safety
context: A folding saw is safer and more efficient than a hatchet for most camp wood; both need a clear swing zone and a stable work position. Also called hatchet safety, folding saw, chopping wood safely, axe safety. Look for a clear arc with no people or branches; wood on a stable base, not held by your foot. Saw dead, down wood, kneel or stand so a missed swing goes into the ground, and sheath tools when done.

title: Winter travel gear
context: Winter trails need traction such as microspikes or snowshoes, insulated boots, extra layers, and more daylight planning. Also called snowshoes, microspikes, ice cleats, winter hiking gear. Look for ice under snow on trails; deep snow that makes you posthole. Carry traction, a warm spare layer, an insulated bottle, and a headlamp, and turn back early.

title: Phone battery and backup power
context: A phone drains fast in cold and when searching for signal; a charged power bank and battery-saving settings keep it working for calls and maps. Also called phone battery dying, power bank, save phone battery, charge phone outdoors. Look for battery level and temperature; airplane mode when you don't need signal. Keep the phone warm in an inside pocket, turn on low-power or airplane mode, dim the screen, and carry a charged power bank.

title: Satellite SOS and messengers
context: Satellite SOS devices and some phones can send an emergency message from places with no cell signal; a personal locator beacon alerts search and rescue directly. Also called satellite SOS, personal locator beacon, PLB, inReach, emergency beacon. Look for a clear view of the sky; the device registered and tested before the trip. Learn how to send an SOS before you need it, keep it on your body, and use it only for real emergencies.

title: Whistle and signal mirror
context: A whistle carries farther than your voice and takes little energy; a signal mirror flashes sunlight to aircraft or searchers miles away. Also called emergency whistle, signal mirror, three whistle blasts. Look for three blasts or three flashes as a distress signal; a whistle on the pack strap or jacket. Blow three blasts and repeat; aim the mirror flash at aircraft or distant searchers using your fingers as a sight.

title: Insect repellent and tick-treated clothing
context: EPA-registered repellents such as DEET, picaridin, or oil of lemon eucalyptus on skin, and permethrin on clothing, reduce tick and mosquito bites. Also called bug spray, DEET, permethrin, picaridin, mosquito repellent. Look for the EPA registration on the label; permethrin for clothes and gear, never skin. Use repellent on exposed skin as the label directs, treat boots and pants with permethrin, and do a tick check after.

title: How much water to carry
context: How much water you need depends on heat, effort, and distance; a rough start is about a half liter per hour of moderate hiking, more in heat. Also called how much water hiking, water bottles, hydration bladder. Look for dark urine or thirst; hot, dry, or high-altitude conditions. Carry enough to reach the next sure source plus extra, and a filter or tablets to treat more.
